name: RightStart Mathematics
line: In RightStart an adult teaches each lesson with an abacus. In AMP, teaching and assessment happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs RightStart Mathematics: an adult teaches each lesson with an abacus and card games. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: RightStart Mathematics is a print program in which an adult teaches each lesson from a manual, with an abacus and card games, in the manual's day-by-day order [1][2]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer is checked and explained, updates the learner's level and sets the next problem.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. RightStart places a child with a short online questionnaire that the adult answers about what the child can do, which gives one starting level, and with written tests for children switching programs [4]. After that, lessons follow the manual's day-by-day order [1].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In RightStart the unit is the lesson, which the adult teaches from a manual with the Cotter Abacus and other materials, followed by card games for practice [1][6]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [16].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once, and repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. RightStart names mastery as a goal and describes it as understanding, with no stated rule for when a lesson counts as learned [3]. Lessons follow the manual's order, and the child advances at their own pace [1][2].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In RightStart, review comes mainly through card games, with few review worksheets [1]. Review lessons open Levels B to F for students new to its second edition [5]. The company holds that understanding reduces the need for review [3]. We found no schedule for when a skill comes back in the pages we read [1][3][5]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [17].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math and runs from counting through precalculus in one program, on one map of skills. A learner further along in geometry than in place value gets work at both levels. RightStart places a child at one level, A through H, in place of grades, and Levels G and H are its middle school course [2][4][5].

rows.range: Levels A through H in place of grades. Levels G and H are its middle school course [2][5].
rows.start: A short online questionnaire the adult answers about what the child can do gives one starting level. Written tests for children switching programs [4].
rows.teaching: The adult teaches each lesson from a manual with the Cotter Abacus and other materials, then the child practices through card games [1][6].
rows.next: The next lesson in the manual's day-by-day order. The child advances at their own pace [1][2].
rows.mastery: Named as a goal and described as understanding. No stated rule for when a lesson counts as learned [3].
rows.review: Mainly through card games, with few review worksheets. Review lessons open Levels B to F [1][5].
rows.print: Print is the core: lesson manual, worksheets, appendix pages and card decks. The same pages for every child [6][7].
rows.adult: Teaches every lesson, plays the practice games and chooses the starting level [1][4].
rows.reports: None found in the pages we read [1][10].
rows.evidence: One small Finnish kindergarten comparison: no significant difference from usual teaching [11]. A nine-child pilot with no comparison group [12]. No Evidence for ESSA or WWC entry found [13][14].

theirs: RightStart Mathematics comes from Activities for Learning, which describes itself as a family-owned business [8]. The curriculum grew out of Joan Cotter's doctoral dissertation, according to the company [9]. The home-school program runs in Levels A through H in place of grades. A child begins at the level that fits and advances at their own pace [2][5].

The adult leads each lesson from a manual that guides the teacher day by day, with the Cotter Abacus, a two-sided abacus grouped in fives and tens, and other materials [1][6]. Practice comes mostly through card games, with no flash cards and few review worksheets [1]. The company holds that math should be taught so that "95% is understood and only 5% memorized" [3].
credit: Hands-on teaching with the Cotter Abacus, grouped in fives and tens, and other materials a child can hold [1][6].
Fact practice through card games with an adult at the table, in place of flash cards [1].
A What Works Clearinghouse practice guide rates concrete and semi-concrete representations as strong evidence for elementary students who struggle in math [15].

theirs: Researchers at the University of Helsinki and the Niilo Mäki Institute in Finland compared RightStart with usual kindergarten teaching (Mononen, Aunio and Koponen, 2014) [11]. It compared classrooms, without random assignment: 38 children taught with RightStart and 32 taught as usual. The RightStart classes covered about 36 of the manual's 87 lessons. Both groups improved in counting, comparing numbers and addition facts. There was no statistically significant difference between the groups after the lessons, or at a follow-up in first grade. The authors call the sample small and ask that the results be read with caution [11].

A second paper from the same team followed nine children with specific language impairment, taught with RightStart for seven months, beside 32 typically developing peers [12]. The nine began with weaker skills. After the lessons their counting did not differ significantly from the peers', and in first grade they matched them in some skills and not in others. There was no group of similar children taught another way [12].

We found no entry for RightStart Mathematics in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [13][14]. The company's research page lists the two Finnish papers and a summary by Joan Cotter [9].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [16]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [17]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want to teach each math lesson yourself, at the table, with an abacus and card games.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want every answer checked as it is given, with the worked steps.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice, set by your learner's own answers.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or past middle school math.
You want daily math that no adult needs to plan, teach or grade.

questions.question: How is AMP different from RightStart Mathematics?
questions.answer: In RightStart an adult teaches each lesson from a manual with an abacus, practice comes through card games, and lessons follow the manual's order [1][2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer is checked, explained and sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does RightStart Mathematics work?
questions.answer: One small Finnish kindergarten study compared it with usual teaching and found no statistically significant difference between the groups [11]. A nine-child pilot had no comparison group [12]. We found no entry in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [13][14].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. An adult can keep teaching RightStart lessons with the abacus, and AMP places the learner from their first answers, whatever level the books are on.
